title: Write with hygiene: temp in the destination dir, verify your own write, then atomic-rename once
summary: The reliable pattern for producing a file good enough to publish is: build the content in a temporary file placed in the same directory as the target (so the final rename is atomic on the same filesystem), verify what you just wrote (existence, and ideally size/hash), and on any failure clean up the temp and abort without touching the target. Straight writes that publish directly risk leaving a truncated or partially-escaped artifact if interrupted.
technique: mktemp with a precise template in the target dir; fill it in one succeeded redirect, checking the return of the fill; run a status/integrity check on the temp BEFORE moving; only then mv; clean the temp on every failure and set restrictive permissions for private material.
evidence_note: queuebash.sh:9061-9088 creates `...candidate.XXXXXX`, fills it with quoted exports (using %q), runs a file-status check, and only then `mv` to the destination, removing the temp on each failure branch. The env/hand-off contract in docs/IPC.md uses the same temp-then-mv then a verify because a partial file would wrongly satisfy a consumer.
invariants: Build the candidate inside the destination directory, not somewhere you must move across filesystems from.
Verify your own output (existence and integrity) before you let it be seen as authoritative.
Publish with one atomic rename (mv) once the temp passes checks; never write to the final name incrementally.
Clean up the temp on every failure, and use an EXIT trap when verification can fail at many points.
For sensitive material set a restrictive umask/permissions during the private write, then relax only the result you deliberately make public.
